content:
Apple has submitted a proposal regarding the fees it can charge for transactions that bypass the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Below are the details of the proposal.

Apple submits proposal for commission on transactions bypassing App Store mechanism

After multiple requests to stay the district court proceedings to clarify how much (or whether) Apple can charge for transactions that bypass the App Store's in-app purchase (IAP) system, Apple has finally formally filed its proposal, outlining a suggested fee structure.

Apple's submission of the proposal comes right as the Supreme Court denied its request to stay the lower court proceedings. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether Apple should be held in contempt for allegedly violating a court order by charging a 27% commission on transactions that bypass the App Store. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers previously issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

Apple argued before the lower court and the Supreme Court that the Supreme Court's ruling could affect the outcome of the proceedings to determine the fees, and that such proceedings should therefore be stayed pending the Supreme Court's decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the lower court to continue advancing the proceedings while the case is being heard.

Accordingly, the proposal Apple submitted today suggests the following fees:

15% for general apps (currently the IAP commission rate is 30%); 10% for the Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals; 5% for apps under the Small Business Programme.

Apple stated: "Factual and expert evidence supporting the above proposed commission rates has been submitted simultaneously." The company added:

Apple also pointed out that its "proposed outbound commission rate is comparable to commission rates of other similar app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also mentioned that "Google Play Store's outbound fee is 20% standard, 15% programme, 10% subscription — a rate that Epic has already agreed to accept."

Apple stated that the company still believes the proceedings to determine the fees should be stayed while the Supreme Court considers the case, and that this submission is only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also noted that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket ban on charging commissions on outbound transactions, holding that such commissions only become problematic when they actually have a deterrent effect.

The proposal has been formally filed, and Epic will have an opportunity to respond. Apple is expected to submit its arguments to the Supreme Court by September 14.
